items.q: Walk through a Gradle build's phases. When does configuration happen, and how does the task graph get built?
shortAnswer: Every Gradle build runs initialization, configuration, then execution, in that fixed order.
Configuration evaluates every project's build script and builds the task graph from declared dependencies. Execution then runs only the tasks that graph needs.
Up-to-date checks run at execution time. A task with unchanged declared inputs and outputs is skipped as UP-TO-DATE instead of re-run.
items.answer:
#### The three phases
A Gradle build runs initialization, configuration, then execution. Initialization reads the settings file and creates a Project per module; configuration evaluates every build script and builds the task graph; execution runs the selected tasks in dependency order. Configuration must finish before any task runs.

#### Configuration is not the work
Configuration is where tasks and properties are registered, not where the build's work happens. Resolving a configuration, reading a file, or printing during configuration runs on every build even when a task is up to date — which is why lazy registration with tasks.register beats eager create, and why heavy work belongs in a task action.

#### The task graph
Gradle builds a directed acyclic graph from declared task dependencies plus the requested tasks, and rejects circular dependencies. Task configuration avoidance means only tasks reachable from the request get configured at all.

#### Up-to-date
During execution Gradle compares each task's declared inputs and outputs against the previous build; unchanged means UP-TO-DATE and the action is skipped. An undeclared input is simply untracked, which is how a task silently goes stale and stops being re-executed.

items.q: How do you make a custom Gradle task incremental, and what is the difference between UP-TO-DATE and FROM-CACHE?
shortAnswer: Declare every input and output with `@Input`, `@InputFiles`, `@OutputDirectory` — Gradle can only track what you tell it about.
UP-TO-DATE means this build already ran the task with identical inputs and outputs, so it is skipped. FROM-CACHE means the outputs came back from the build cache and the action never ran.
A task whose outputs don't depend only on declared inputs — like a build timestamp in the output — is not cacheable and should say so.
items.answer:
#### What incremental means
Incremental build lets Gradle reuse a task's previous outputs. After a successful run Gradle snapshots the task's declared inputs and outputs; if the next run finds them unchanged, the task is skipped as UP-TO-DATE and its actions never execute.

#### Declaring inputs and outputs
A custom task is only trackable if it declares them: @Input for scalar values, @InputFiles/@InputDirectory for files, @OutputDirectory/@OutputFile for results, using abstract Property or ConfigurableFileCollection so configuration stays lazy. An undeclared input silently breaks the guarantee in the dangerous direction — the task is skipped when it should have run. Input normalization (line endings, property-file ordering, ABI signatures on compile classpaths) raises the hit rate without weakening correctness.

#### UP-TO-DATE versus FROM-CACHE
UP-TO-DATE means this build already ran the task with identical inputs and outputs on this machine. FROM-CACHE means the outputs were restored from the build cache by input hash — the action never executed here, and the entry may have been produced by another machine entirely. Both skip the action; FROM-CACHE additionally survives clean and fresh checkouts.

#### What breaks tracking
Non-deterministic tasks — an output stamped with a build timestamp, or an output depending on an undeclared value — must not be cacheable, and Gradle disables tracking when it cannot prove determinism. A task that never shows UP-TO-DATE is leaking an input; that is the debugging signal.

traps: Believing every task is automatically incremental — a custom task with no declared inputs/outputs never goes UP-TO-DATE.
Mixing up the two outcomes: UP-TO-DATE is local incremental state, FROM-CACHE is a cache restore and can come from another machine.

items.q: What does the Gradle configuration cache actually store, and which build logic breaks it?
shortAnswer: It stores the finished task graph and configuration on disk, so a later build skips configuration entirely when the build inputs haven't changed.
Logic that reads mutable external state during configuration — a timestamp, a random value, a file, a raw env read — breaks serialization and forces a miss or a failure.
It's the preferred mode since Gradle 9.0 and becomes the default in Gradle 10, so fixing violations now is the migration.
items.answer:
#### What it stores
The configuration cache serializes the output of the configuration phase: the task graph, task configuration, and declared inputs. On the next build Gradle checks the configuration inputs — build scripts, buildSrc and included builds, version catalogs, gradle.properties — and if none changed it loads the stored graph and goes straight to execution, skipping configuration entirely.

#### What breaks it
Serialization means every object captured during configuration must survive storage and deserialization in a fresh VM, and environment state must be declared. Violations are the classic ones: reading a timestamp or random value during configuration, reading files directly, touching another project's state, using deprecated listeners such as TaskExecutionListener, and storing a Project or Gradle instance in a task field. Each produces a report you can read; the build fails when the violation is real, or warns during adoption.

#### Why it matters now
Since Gradle 9.0 the configuration cache is the preferred mode of execution, and Gradle 10 makes it the default. It also unlocks parallel execution of independent tasks within a single project. It is separate from the build cache: this one removes configuration time, the other removes execution time, and they compose. Budget the first adoption as a dedicated task — run with problem reporting on, fix each item, and add a CI gate that fails new violations.

items.q: When is a remote build cache actually worth running, and when does it add nothing?
shortAnswer: A remote cache pays off when many builds produce identical outputs from identical inputs — CI compiling the same dependency set across branches and machines is the ideal case.
It adds nothing when builds rarely repeat inputs: a mostly-serial single-module app, or tasks stamped with a unique timestamp that changes the cache key every run.
The win depends on what is cached. Compile and merge tasks cache well; tests usually should not be cached, and non-hermetic tasks cannot.
items.answer:
#### How it works
With org.gradle.caching=true every task's outputs are stored under a key derived from the task implementation and its declared, normalized inputs. A later build with the same key skips the action and restores the output — labeled FROM-CACHE. The local cache lives in the Gradle user home; the remote cache is an HTTP/HTTPS service shared across machines.

#### When it genuinely helps
The economics are: how often does another build produce identical inputs, and how expensive is the task? CI is the sweet spot — many branches and jobs compile the same dependency set, so one build populates and the rest restore compile and dex outputs. Developers benefit the same way across branches and after a fresh checkout. AGP tasks cache well when inputs are normalized; R8 and merged resources are cacheable when stable.

#### When it adds nothing
A build that rarely repeats inputs — one module, mostly serial, tasks salted with a per-build timestamp — gets only the I/O cost. A timestamp inside an output changes the key on every run, so the task never hits. Path-dependent or unnormalized inputs also break keys between machines.

#### What to exclude
Tests should not be cached: restored test results hide flakes and skip real execution. Keep isPush=false on developer machines so CI owns the cache, read the hit rate from a build scan, and only then call it a win.

items.q: How does Gradle parallelize builds, and what was configuring-on-demand trying to save?
shortAnswer: Parallel execution runs independent tasks in different projects at the same time on separate workers. With the configuration cache, even independent tasks inside one project run in parallel.
Configuring-on-demand skipped projects the current invocation didn't need, but it was deprecated because it assumed the project graph was predictable.
The modern replacement is the configuration cache plus isolated projects. Together they make partial and cached configuration safe.
items.answer:
#### Parallel execution
org.gradle.parallel=true runs tasks that do not depend on each other across modules on separate workers at the same time; with the configuration cache enabled, independent tasks inside one project also run in parallel. Dependency chains stay serial, so the critical path is unchanged — a single fat module serializes the whole build regardless.

#### Configuring-on-demand
Without it, Gradle configures every project in the build even when the invocation touches two. Configuring-on-demand instead configures only the projects on the path of the requested tasks plus their dependencies, which saves real time at scale. Gradle deprecated it in 7.0 because it assumed the project graph was predictable: a plugin reading another project's state during configuration silently broke under partial configuration, and it still re-ran configuration on every invocation.

#### The modern replacement
The configuration cache serializes configuration per invocation, and isolated projects gives each project strict boundaries — no project may touch another's mutable state — which makes partial configuration safe. On a cache miss only the affected projects reconfigure instead of the whole graph. For a large Android codebase the target state is: parallel workers, cached configuration, and enforced module boundaries rather than assumed ones.

items.q: Why does running a clean build 'to be safe' usually make a build worse, not better?
shortAnswer: Clean deletes every task output, so the next build has nothing to compare and every task re-runs from scratch. All incremental state is gone.
The build cache survives clean because its keys are input hashes, but local up-to-date state and file snapshots are lost, so tasks pay a restore instead of a skip.
A build that needs clean to be correct has a real bug — a task wrongly staying UP-TO-DATE — and deleting outputs hides it instead of finding it.
items.answer:
#### What clean destroys
clean deletes the build directory, so every task's previous outputs are gone. The next run cannot compare inputs and outputs, nothing is UP-TO-DATE, and every task re-executes — in a large project, minutes of work the incremental build would have skipped.

#### Cache survives, incremental state does not
The build cache is keyed by input hashes and stored in the Gradle user home, so clean followed by a cache-enabled build still restores outputs as FROM-CACHE. What clean throws away is the local incremental state — prior outputs and file snapshots — so tasks now pay a restore step instead of a skip, and the local cache misses entirely.

#### The habit is a symptom
People clean because a build was wrong once: a task stayed UP-TO-DATE when it should have run. That is a misdeclared input or output, and the fix is to declare the real input, not to delete outputs forever. A CI pipeline that cleans first discards every benefit the caches exist to provide. Use clean deliberately to diagnose or repackage; if a build needs it to be correct, find and fix the task instead.

items.q: AGP 9 no longer needs org.jetbrains.kotlin.android. What actually changed, and what breaks if you keep applying it?
shortAnswer: AGP 9.0 ships built-in Kotlin. Applying `com.android.application` or `com.android.library` now compiles Kotlin itself, so the separate Kotlin Android plugin is neither needed nor allowed.
AGP carries its own Kotlin Gradle plugin runtime — KGP 2.2.10 minimum at 9.0. kapt is incompatible, so processors move to KSP, or `com.android.legacy-kapt` as a stopgap.
The new DSL is also the default: `android.kotlinOptions` moves to `kotlin.compilerOptions`, and the opt-out flags are removed in AGP 10.
items.answer:
#### What AGP 9 changed
AGP 9.0 introduced built-in Kotlin: applying com.android.application or com.android.library now compiles Kotlin itself, so org.jetbrains.kotlin.android is neither required nor allowed. AGP carries a runtime dependency on the Kotlin Gradle plugin (KGP 2.2.10 minimum at 9.0) and adds the Kotlin standard library automatically, so the AGP and Kotlin toolchains cannot drift. In the current stack, Kotlin 2.4.10 and AGP 9.3.0 work together out of the box.

#### What breaks
Applying the old plugin fails with 'the org.jetbrains.kotlin.android plugin is no longer required'. kapt is incompatible with built-in Kotlin: migrate processors to KSP, or as a stopgap apply com.android.legacy-kapt at the AGP version. android.kotlinOptions moves to kotlin.compilerOptions, and jvmTarget now defaults to android.compileOptions.targetCompatibility, so a separately declared jvmTarget becomes a conflict. Extra Kotlin source directories move into android.sourceSets with the kotlin accessor.

#### The migration
Module by module works: keep android.builtInKotlin=false in gradle.properties and apply com.android.built-in-kotlin to the module being migrated, removing both when done. The opt-out flags (builtInKotlin, newDsl) are removed in AGP 10, so the migration is the plan, not a choice. KMP modules stay different: they use org.jetbrains.kotlin.multiplatform with com.android.kotlin.multiplatform.library.

items.q: How do you customize a single build variant without the old applicationVariants API?
shortAnswer: AGP's Variant API gives you three callbacks on the `androidComponents` block — `finalizeDsl`, `beforeVariants`, `onVariants` — each at a different point in variant creation.
`beforeVariants` gives you a `VariantBuilder` where the build flow is still mutable. `onVariants` gives you the finished `Variant`, whose `Property` values resolve lazily at execution.
AGP's own tasks are not public API, so you read and transform outputs through the artifact API instead of hooking tasks by name.
items.answer:
#### The model
The Variant API (stable since AGP 9, incubating since AGP 7) replaces applicationVariants, libraryVariants and variantFilter. All customization goes through the androidComponents block, whose callbacks run during configuration and must stay fast; heavy work belongs in tasks.

#### finalizeDsl
Runs after the android block is evaluated but before variants exist. DSL values can still be changed programmatically; everything must be resolvable at configuration time.

#### beforeVariants
Receives a VariantBuilder, where the build flow is still mutable: disable a variant with vb.enable=false, change minSdk, drop tests. A VariantSelector narrows the callback, for example selector().withBuildType("release").withFlavor("color", "blue").

#### onVariants
Receives the finished Variant. Variants and artifacts are fixed here, so you set Property values — signingConfig, buildConfigFields, manifestPlaceholders — that resolve lazily when tasks execute, and you can wire them to providers from your own tasks.

#### Artifacts, not tasks
AGP tasks are implementation details and must not be hooked by name. Read or transform outputs through the artifact API — component.artifacts.get(SingleArtifact.APK), or transform a MergedManifest. That contract is configuration-cache friendly, which is exactly why AGP 9 removed the old hooks.

traps: Hooking AGP task names or grabbing task instances — they are implementation details and change between versions.
Mutating the VariantBuilder after the callback finishes; by onVariants the variant set is frozen.

items.q: What problem do Gradle version catalogs solve, and how do Compose BOMs fit in?
shortAnswer: A version catalog puts dependency and plugin coordinates in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` and exposes type-safe accessors, so each version lives in exactly one place.
A BOM is different. It's a dependency of constraints that aligns the versions of a whole family during resolution, not just a place to store numbers.
The catalog records intent and the platform enforces it — the pattern is the version in the catalog, then `implementation(platform(libs.compose.bom))`.
items.answer:
#### The catalog
A version catalog centralizes dependency and plugin coordinates in gradle/libs.versions.toml and exposes them as type-safe accessors — libs.compose.bom, libs.plugins.ksp — so a version lives in exactly one place, with IDE autocomplete and a single point for upgrades. It does not affect resolution: a version from the catalog behaves identically to the same version written inline in a module.

#### BOMs and platforms
A BOM is a POM of dependency constraints, and Gradle imports it with the platform modifier. Declaring implementation(platform(libs.compose.bom)) pulls the BOM into the graph and aligns the versions of the whole androidx.compose family, even where a module does not write a version. Plain platform constraints recommend versions and lose to a higher explicit version elsewhere; enforcedPlatform overrides the graph but exports forced versions transitively, so it is a last resort.

#### Together
The current pattern: keep the Compose BOM (2026.06.01) in the catalog, apply it with implementation(platform(...)) in every Compose module, and stop writing per-artifact Compose versions. The catalog records intent; the platform enforces alignment. For libraries you must pin hard, prefer a rich version constraint with strictly over force, which fights every other module in the graph.

items.q: How do you stop a transitive dependency from silently changing, and what is dependency locking?
shortAnswer: By default Gradle resolves to the highest requested version. You steer it with a resolution strategy and constraints, or freeze it with dependency locking.
Locking records each configuration's resolved versions in `gradle.lockfile` and fails the build when resolution would drift from them — that's true reproducibility.
Lock dynamic and changing versions deliberately. Regenerate with `--write-locks` only to upgrade, and review the diff like a code review.
items.answer:
#### How versions win
Gradle resolves to the highest requested version by default. You shape that with the resolution strategy on the configuration and with constraints: force pins one version everywhere but fights the whole graph; failOnVersionConflict makes drift loud instead of silent. The precise tool is a dependency constraint, and rich versions add strictly and require to express rejection as well as preference.

#### What locking is
Dependency locking records the resolved versions of each configuration in gradle.lockfile and verifies on later builds that resolution matches. A new version published, a transitive added, a constraint changed — any drift fails the build instead of silently changing your dependencies. Locked versions behave as strictly, so raising a declared version above the lock also fails until you regenerate. This is what makes reproducible builds real, especially with dynamic versions or in CI where caches can mask drift.

#### The workflow
Enable locking, run once with --write-locks to create gradle.lockfile, commit it, then regenerate only when you intend to upgrade and review the diff as a code review. Lenient lock mode downgrades failures to warnings for experimentation. The distinction to state clearly: the resolution strategy defines the algorithm, locking freezes the outcome.

code.caption: Constraints, a resolution strategy, and locking

followUps: What happens when a declared version goes above the lock state?
Why should changing versions like SNAPSHOT not be locked?

traps: Saying locking 'pins' versions by editing build files — it records resolved output and fails on drift instead.
Assuming the lockfile prevents drift automatically; it must be committed and enforced in CI to mean anything.
